items.title: Five Remaining Reasons to Eat: From Simple Hunger to Healing the Body Already Harmed

items.zh: 如是受用，身無沈重，有所堪能，堪任修斷；令心速疾得三摩地；令入出息無有艱難；令心不為惛沈睡眠之所纏擾。如是名為無艱難存養。若由有艱難存養，壽命得存，身得安住，此名有罪，亦有染污。若由無艱難存養，壽命得存，身得安住，此名無罪，亦無染污。諸有多聞聖弟子眾，遠離有罪有染存養，習近無罪無染存養，由是故說為暫支持。問：云何習近如前所說無罪無染所有存養，以自存活？答：若受飲食，為除飢渴、為攝梵行、為斷故受、為令新受當不更生、為當存養力樂無罪安隱而住，如是習近無罪無染所有存養，而自存活。云何名為為除飢渴受諸飲食？謂至食時，多生飢渴，氣力虛羸，希望飲食。為欲息此飢渴纏逼、氣力虛羸，知量而食。如是食已，令於非時不為飢羸之所纏逼，謂於日晚或於夜分，乃至明日未至食時。如是名為為除飢渴受諸飲食。云何名為為攝梵行受諸飲食？謂知其量受諸飲食，由是因緣，修善品者，或於現法、或於此日，飲食已後，身無沈重，有所堪能，堪任修斷；令心速疾得三摩地；令入出息無有艱難；令心不為惛沈睡眠之所纏擾。由是速疾有力有能得所未得、觸所未觸、證所未證。如是名為為攝梵行受諸飲食。云何名為為斷故受受諸飲食？謂如有一，由過去世食不知量、食所匪宜、不消而食；由是因緣，於其身中生起種種身諸疾病，所謂疥癩、皰漿、瘶等，如前廣說。由此種種疾病因緣，發生身中極重、猛利、熾然苦惱不可意受。為欲息除如是疾病，及為息除從此因緣所生苦受，習近種種良醫所說饒益所宜隨順醫藥，及受種種悅意飲食。
items.en: Eaten in this way, the body does not grow heavy, remains capable, fit for cultivation; the mind swiftly attains concentration; the in-breath and out-breath are not laboured; the mind is not entangled by dullness and drowsiness. This is called nourishment that is not difficult. …If one eats in order to remove hunger and thirst, to support pure conduct, to end the old feeling [of illness], to prevent new feeling [of illness] from arising, and to preserve the strength, ease, and blameless, peaceful abiding needed — cultivating, in this way, nourishment free of fault and free of defilement — one sustains one's own life properly. …When mealtime arrives, great hunger and thirst commonly arise, strength grows weak, and one longs for food. In order to put an end to this affliction of hunger and thirst and this weakness, one eats according to the proper measure. …Eating according to the proper measure, for this reason, one who cultivates wholesome practice … the body does not grow heavy, remains capable, fit for cultivation; the mind swiftly attains concentration … and, through this, swiftly gains the strength and capacity to attain what has not been attained, to touch what has not been touched, to realise what has not been realised. …It is like one who, through not knowing the proper measure in past eating, eating what was unsuitable, or eating before what was already eaten had digested, thereby gives rise to various bodily illnesses … in order to put an end to such illness, and to the painful sensation arising from it, one draws near to whatever beneficial and suitable medicine a good physician prescribes, and to whatever pleasing food is appropriate.

items.zh: 由此能斷已生疾病，及彼因緣所生苦受。如是名為為斷故受受諸飲食。云何名為為令新受當不更生受諸飲食？
items.en: By this one is able to end illness that has already arisen, together with the painful feeling produced by it as its cause and condition. This is called receiving food in order to end old feeling. What is called receiving food so that new feeling will not arise?

items.title: Section: Every Motivation for Eating Closes, and Two Summaries Distil the Whole Teaching

items.zh: 謂如有一，由現在世安樂無病、氣力具足，不非量食、不食匪宜、亦非不消而更重食，令於未來食住身中成不消病，或於身中當生隨一身諸疾病，所謂疥癩、皰漿、瘶等，如前廣說。由是因緣，當生身中如前所說種種苦受，餘如前說。如是名為為令新受當不更生受諸飲食。云何名為為當存養力樂無罪安隱而住受諸飲食？謂飲食已，壽命得存，是名存養。若除飢羸，是名為力。若斷故受，新受不生，是名為樂。若以正法追求飲食，不染、不愛，乃至廣說而受用之，是名無罪。若受食已，身無沈重，有所堪能，堪任修斷，如前廣說，如是名為安隱而住。是故說言：由正思擇食於所食，不為倡蕩、不為憍逸、不為飾好、不為端嚴，乃至廣說。是名廣辨於食知量。云何應知此中略義？謂若所受食，若如是食，當知總名此中略義。何者所食？謂諸段食。即餅、麨、飯、羹、臛、糜、粥，如前廣說。云何而食？謂正思擇食於所食，不為倡蕩、不為憍逸、不為飾好、不為端嚴，乃至廣說。復次，應知此中略義，謂為攝受對治，為遠離欲樂行邊，為遠離自苦行邊，為攝受梵行，受諸飲食。云何為攝受對治受諸飲食？
items.en: It is like one who, presently at ease and free of illness, with strength fully intact, does not eat beyond measure … so that, in the future, undigested food lodging in the body does not become a source of illness, nor gives rise to any of the various bodily ailments already named. This is called eating so that new feeling [of illness] will not arise. …Having eaten, life is preserved — this is called preservation. Removing hunger and weakness is called strength. Ending the old feeling [of illness] and preventing new feeling from arising is called ease. Seeking food through proper means, and receiving it without attachment or craving — as explained at length — is called blamelessness. Having eaten, the body is not heavy, remains capable, fit for cultivation — this is called peaceful abiding. It is therefore said: through correct discernment in eating what is eaten — not for wanton pleasure, not for pride, not for grooming, not for elegance, and so on at length — this is called the full explanation of moderation in eating. …What is received as food, and how it is eaten — this, in total, should be understood as the summary meaning here. …Furthermore, the summary meaning here should be understood as: eating in order to counteract affliction, in order to avoid the extreme of indulgence, in order to avoid the extreme of self-mortification, and in order to support pure conduct.

blocks.text: The good reasons for eating, and two summaries that tie the whole teaching together.

Food eaten properly leaves "the body not heavy, and the mind swiftly attains concentration". Master Cháng Bǎi: very spicy, sour, salty, or bitter food makes concentration difficult. Venerable Miào Jìng suggests that long-term meditators keep a food record, because some of what appears in meditation comes from food.

One eats: to remove hunger and thirst; to support the holy life; to heal past illness; to prevent new illness; and to preserve strength, ease, blamelessness, and peaceful abiding. Master Cháng Bǎi: 故受 ("old feeling") is the pain of illness already present; "new feeling" is illness that excess would bring.

"Removing hunger and weakness is strength; healing past illness and preventing new illness is ease." The second summary: one eats "in order to counteract affliction, to avoid the extreme of indulgence, to avoid the extreme of self-mortification, and to support the holy life". Venerable Miào Jìng: 攝受 here means learning to correct one's own faults.

These five reasons are still recited before meals in many monasteries. For a lay reader, the point carries over directly: eat for strength and health, not for display, and notice how food affects the mind.

quiz.q: After nourishment that is not difficult, how are body and mind, and what food does Master Cháng Bǎi say helps concentration?
options: body not heavy, mind swiftly concentrated, breath easy; light, easily digested food
quiz.why: Eaten in this way, the body is not heavy and the mind swiftly attains concentration. Master Cháng Bǎi: very spicy, sour, salty, or bitter food makes concentration hard; light, easily digested food makes it easier.

quiz.q: What does Venerable Miào Jìng say about the link between meditation experiences and food?
options: some of them come from food
quiz.why: Venerable Miào Jìng: some of what appears during sitting meditation comes from food — which is why he suggests long-term meditators keep a food record.

quiz.q: What purposes of eating does the treatise list for faultless, undefiled nourishment, and how does Master Cháng Bǎi distinguish "blameworthy" from "defiled"?
options: for looks and fun; the same thing

to remove hunger and thirst, support pure conduct, heal past illness, prevent new illness, and preserve strength, ease, and blameless peace; blame concerns improper sources, defilement the six marks in eating
quiz.why: "If one eats in order to remove hunger and thirst, to support pure conduct, to heal past illness, to prevent new illness from arising." Master Cháng Bǎi: blame refers to food obtained improperly; defilement refers to the six marks of attachment in eating it.

quiz.q: The English renders 為斷故受 as "to heal past illness." How do the lectures read 故受?
options: the painful feeling produced by illness — "illness-feeling" — caused by past immoderate eating
quiz.why: Master Cháng Bǎi: 故受 is the feeling of illness. Venerable Miào Jìng: past immoderate eating brought on much pain in the body. The text itself speaks of ending the illness and the painful feeling it produces; the English renders 受 simply as "illness," losing the sense of painful feeling.

quiz.q: What does the treatise call removing hunger and weakness?
quiz.why: "Removing hunger and weakness is called strength." Venerable Miào Jìng: food that relieves hunger and weakness gives the body strength — that is "strength."

quiz.q: Healing past illness and preventing new illness is called "ease." How does Master Cháng Bǎi explain this?
options: ease is not having to work
everyone is unhappy when ill; eating that ends old illness and prevents new illness is called ease
quiz.why: "Healing past illness and preventing new illness from arising is called ease." Master Cháng Bǎi: no one is happy when ill; eating that removes the old ailment and produces no new one is called ease.

quiz.q: In the second summary, eating serves which four purposes?
options: counteracting affliction, avoiding indulgence, avoiding self-mortification, supporting pure conduct
quiz.why: "Eating in order to counteract affliction, in order to avoid the extreme of indulgence, in order to avoid the extreme of self-mortification, and in order to support pure conduct." Master Cháng Bǎi on avoiding self-mortification: not tormenting oneself with austerities of not eating or drinking.
